Sparse attention fixes memory bandwidth, not memory capacity.

“The whole idea of HiCache is trying to offload KV cache from the HBM to a lower tier, higher capacity but lower bandwidth memory, and only load the most relevant set of tokens during computation.”

“Sparse attention doesn’t mitigate the memory capacity bottleneck. It’s a technique that helps a lot with memory bandwidth.”

“During the sparse attention computation, you still need to select the tokens. So you still have to keep all the tokens in context, and you cannot discard them. At some point, it still has to be loaded into HBM.”

“That’s where HiSparse becomes useful, because it can apply the typical caching rules so that you could load the most relevant parts into HBM.”

Borrowing an idea from one research discipline to solve a thorny problem in another is an age-old scientific trick. Charles Darwin’s theory of natural selection, for example, famously inspired algorithms in computer science that “evolve” solutions to complex problems.

But such clever leaps are fleetingly rare. For #AI, however, hopping between fields can be a breeze.

Researchers highlighted that ability with the release of 36 preprints produced with a single suite of AI tools called BootLoops. The so-called harness can be used with any large language model, such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

And in just 3 months, researchers used Claude outfitted with BootLoops to cross-pollinate at a massive scale, spotting—and precisely solving—problems in seemingly unrelated fields that share the same mathematical structures.

The resulting papers range widely, from figuring out the age of sunspots, to analyzing government health policies, to attempting to decipher a mysterious medieval manuscript.

Learn more: https://t.co/r5iy80T5Hk

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

This is a great set of observations. I agree with almost of them. It’s great that Arpit got to spend a couple of days inside Anthropic but I also think it’s interesting/reassuring that most of these observations could’ve been made without spending any time inside Anthropic at all. 

Personally I am intrigued by how one comes to the assessment of how many months we are from RSI based on the amount of code Anthropic researchers are writing with the help of AI. But I’m open minded about their/Arpit’s intuition.

I also find the following comment insightful for the long term economics of the frontier AI labs:

“We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier.”
